Core Concept, Examples, Reading Strategies, and Traps are present. Both visual-dependent examples include their own drawable placeholders and text square charts. Assumptions and Filipino inference additions appear.
Inference is defined with clues in three short sentences; evidence, premise, assumption, legend, unit, and scale receive plain explanations. No old abstract finance language remains.
Infer is defined at the opening; Filipino paghatol is explained as checking whether a statement has enough support before its application.
No teaching analogy is used.

All ten examples contain explicit questions, supplied passages or charts, and simple worked solutions. The bar-chart legend is necessary problem-specific data; assumption terminology is taught in Core Concept instead of supplied as the answer in its question.
No repeated exam claims or exam-opening phrases occur.
The Filipino section and examples #8–10 use short Filipino explanations of clues, the whole-paragraph message, and evidence limits.
Hinuha, pangunahing diwa, and paghatol receive English glosses at first definition. No further hard Filipino grammar term requires a gloss.
Examples #8–10 teach the Filipino portion using Filipino passages, prompts, and solutions. English examples serve the separate English teaching.

findings.problem: Example 7 gives all three scale conversions inline without displayed key computations. The steps are understandable, so this is a minor formatting failure rather than missing reasoning.

checked: The displayed computations 6 times 5 equals 30, 3 times 5 equals 15, and 30 minus 15 equals 15 are all narrow single-operation lines.
Teaching paragraphs have one to three short sentences. Chart rows are short separate labels, and numbered lists are confined to worked solutions.

Both one-line placeholders specify title, axes, zero origin, step size, all three labeled values; the second adds the threshold line. Each is independently drawable. The text square chart supplies usable data before rendering.

Inference, evidence, premise, argument conclusion, necessary assumption, legend, unit, scale, hinuha, main idea and evaluation are explained before examples need them. Trading volume has been removed.

Teaching shows how to connect evidence, compare claim strength, negate an assumption while holding premises fixed, translate squares through scale, combine a note with values, and form Filipino whole-passage judgments.

Explicit limits cover possible versus supported claims, direct facts versus requested inferences, useful versus necessary assumptions, reasoning validity versus accidental truth, counts versus causes, single-result generalization, and chart notes versus graph-only conclusions.
